newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-CONCERN IN FORMULA ONE OVER TOBACCO THREAT.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-CONCERN IN FORMULA ONE OVER TOBACCO THREAT.

text.p: Formula One teams expressed concern over the ban on sponsorship of sporting events by tobacco companies announced on Monday by Britain's new Labour government.
Motor racing's top outfits are heavily supported by cigarette manufacturers, including McLaren, Benetton, Williams and Jordan, and could be forced to search for alternative financial backing.

Ian Phillips, commercial director of Jordan Grand Prix, conceded the matter was of concern to the team, but pointed out that tobacco advertising had not been carried on their cars in Britain for a number of seasons.
"We have not advertised tobacco in Britain for a few years now because of television," he said.
"But at the moment it's a gentleman's agreement with the tobacco companies. We abide by what they say and therefore do not show the tobacco names on our cars in Britain."
John Postlethwaite, marketing director of the Benetton team, said he did not expect the ban to have any dire effects on Formula One teams.

"We have been aware of the possibilities for some time," he said. "I cannot see it being too serious for the sport as a whole. There are many other sponsors and everyone has a wide spread of sponsors involved."
Max Mosley, president of the International Automobile Federation (FIA), said the legislation was a matter of concern to him.
"We are the world governing body and this is a problem in one country," he said. "The Government is aware of our position."

Earlier this season, the Canadian Grand Prix had come under threat when the country's government proposed a similar ban on tobacco advertising, although an amendment was eventually passed which excluded the Formula One race.

At the time, Formula One supremo Bernie Ecclestone had threatened to drop the race from the calendar. "For us it won't be a problem," he said. "We have half a dozen countries asking us to stage a race for them.
There was a cautious reaction from golf's European Tour whose British programme has just one tobacco-sponsored event, the recently staged Benson and Hedges International at the Oxfordshire course.

Tour executive director Ken Schofield said: "We have had this speculation before. We are probably a little different from other sports in that we trade in about 20 different countries, so we are familiar with the situation.

"For some years we have been unable to accept tobacco and alcohol sponsors in numerous continental European countries. We must now wait to see how this progresses, but we have always been law-abiding."
